utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, your microphone. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, the lesser of the two nations in this Court, together with Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you, too. Number one, written version of Rule 98 bis decision, we are giving it a final reading today in the afternoon, and hopefully if everything is plain sailing as it should be, then we will follow with the filing. My understanding, Mr. Cunningham, you've got some information to exchange with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. First of all with respect to our trial schedule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Chuqing, could I have these books, these folders put somewhere because they are obstructing. I mean, I don't need to see Mr. Bilo [phoen], for example. He is leaving soon anyway. Thank you, usher. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, there's three things I want to bring up, two in open session and one in private session. The first one is with respect to schedule. It is our belief that the Defence case will end no later than the first week of March, my guess is it'll probably end towards the end of the February, which I think is well within the guidelines that the Court has provided us with. Secondly, Ms. Korner asked me today about reports from experts. Obviously we're well aware of our disclosure obligations, and we will endeavour to do our best to get them all the reports before the Christmas holidays, because I know there's nothing better than reading a report on Christmas day. The third thing I'd like to talk about with the Chamber, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow, we were scheduled to sit in the afternoon, the sitting was shifted to the afternoon in order to accommodate the Blagojevic Trial Chamber. But I'm informed this morning by my secretary that Blagojevic is not sitting tomorrow. The sitting has been cancelled. So if you agree, we could try and shift it to the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were very surprised to hear we were in the afternoon. We thought we were in the mornings all week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was actually Blagojevic had a witness that they were trying to -- they had problems with a witness apparently, and they asked me to have today and tomorrow shifted to the afternoon. And so it was a compromise. Today we sit in the morning, and tomorrow we sit in the afternoon. But that has also been shifted now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're perfectly happy with the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst I remember, can we take then that next week the witnesses are as on the list, in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There is one scheduling problem. I'll get back to you on it this afternoon. I know the first witness is still scheduled to be the same, but one of them is -- the next witness after that is one of the ones who has had some concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Chuqing, do we have the schedule for January as yet? Do we have the schedule for January, for January? No. Okay. Try to have the sitting of the 14th of January in the afternoon. Okay. So this next witness today is -- any further business before? Okay. So usher, could you bring the witness in, please. Thank you. There are no protective measures here, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a need for a caution? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would have thought not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence. And our Rules require that before you do so, you enter -- you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is being handed to you. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. I want you to feel at ease. You are going -- you have been summoned to give evidence here by Mr. Brdjanin, who is the accused in this trial, as you know. And as a consequence, you're going to be first asked a series of questions by Mr. Cunningham who is representing Mr. Brdjanin here. Mr. Cunningham is the gentleman here in the front row in the middle. He will then be followed by Ms. Korner leading the team for the Prosecution in this case. Ms. Korner will cross-examine you. She'll put to you a set of questions. Now your obligation and your responsibility, according to the Rules and also according to the solemn declaration that you have made a minute ago, is to answer all questions fully and truthfully as possible, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. In other words, you have no right to say "I give preference to the questions being asked by the Defence or by the Prosecution." Your duty is to treat all questions the same and answer them truthfully irrespective of where they are coming from. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We hope to finish with you today. I'm sure that there shouldn't be any problems which would make it possible to you to return back to Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- with your family again. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Drenkja Beric?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Beric, Drenkja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What municipality were you born in?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What municipality do you currently live in?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Also Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you work?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you work for?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I'm with the health ministry at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of work do you do for the health ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I'm an administrator for protocol and files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How long have you worked for the Ministry of Health?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Since the 1st of February 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever work for the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: This was from the 13th of July 1992 until the 13th of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you work for? Who was your boss?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I was Mr. Brdjanin's secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back in July of 1992, had you been -- who were you working for specifically before July 13th, 1992? Were you working for the municipality of Banja Luka? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I was employed there until the beginning of April 1992. I was with a secretariat as a typist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long had you been working for the -- let's put it this way: When did you first start working for the Municipality of Banja Luka? What year?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: 1986, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work continuously for the municipality from 1986 through 1992, or were there periods of time when you were not working for them?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of such interruptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to July 13th, 1992, when you started working for Mr. Brdjanin. What was your job title?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Technical secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did your duties include?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: To answer the phone, to call people whenever Mr. Brdjanin tells me to do so, to type up letters whenever that was necessary. That was about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Brdjanin have an office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two offices, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When was -- where were these offices located at? Which building?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: The building was called the solidarity centre, but the offices actually belonged to the Chamber of Commerce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us there were two offices. Describe if you can what the offices looked like. First of all, was there a corridor, a hallway, that led to the offices?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a corridor. And outside the corridor, there was a small hall from which there was a door leading first to my room. And then from my room into Mr. Brdjanin's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how far was your desk from Mr. Brdjanin's desk in terms of feet or metres? How far away were you?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Not more than 5 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your office, could you hear what was going on in Mr. Brdjanin's office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could, especially when the temperatures were high, Mr. Brdjanin would keep the door to his office open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you worked from 13 July to 13 September. Are those the hot months in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- the summer of 1992, July through September, were you able to use any air-conditioning in your office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No. There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that I did some typing for Mr. Brdjanin. What sort of equipment did you have to type on?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: A mechanical typewriter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your job include serving as a receptionist? Meaning if people would come calling on Mr. Brdjanin, to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Well, first people would enter my office, and they would speak to me to see if they would be allowed to see Mr. Brdjanin, to see if he was there to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically, in this two-month period that you worked for Mr. Brdjanin, what were your hours of work? What time did you go to work in the morning? What time did you leave at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I started at 8.00 in the morning and stayed until 1500 hours in the afternoon, but I used to come in early, which was considered normal. And sometimes when I needed to stay late, I would just stay late for as long as it took to finish my work. Sometimes I'd stay half an hour late, but not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what time would you normally get to the office and start working? 8.00?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: That's when my work began, at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did Mr. Brdjanin typically get to work?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: He would be there at 8.00 punctually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would arrive there at 8.00, would there be anyone waiting in the hallway outside the office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were people there almost every morning who came to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And typically, how many people would be there each morning waiting to see Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: At least 20 people. Sometimes more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know as the people were lined up what their ethnicity was? Did you ask them or look at IDs or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No. I never knew who exactly was waiting in front of the door. In terms of their ethnicity, we didn't keep any lists. We didn't ID people, nor do we call those people over; they just came of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there would -- on a typical day there would be non-Serbs in line seeking help from Mr. Brdjanin in July and September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: As I said, there would be people waiting belonging to all different ethnic groups, but there were no lists kept so we don't know their names. It was only after they told us their names that I could conclude whether they were a Croat or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you just told me, could you conclude back in July to September 1992 whether there were Muslims or Croats waiting to see Mr. Brdjanin when he came to work in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I took her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I took it as such, too, but I wanted to be careful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about typically what would happen with these line of people waiting outside the door? What would Mr. Brdjanin do with these people? Would he see them? Would he tell them to leave? What would happen?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin would see every single person. He would receive them in his office. They would raise their problems, and then he would take them back to my office to write up a brief report concerning their request or whatever assistance it was that they had requested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's break that down step by step. Would the people go into Mr. Brdjanin's office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sorts of things -- were they asking him for help?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of things were they asking for help about? What were the subject matters?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Most people had similar problems regardless of whether they were Muslims, Serbs, or Croats. Normally they would ask for help when they were looking for a job. Housing matters were sometimes a problem. And food also was one of the typical problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the people went into the back office with Mr. Brdjanin and talked with him about these subjects, what would he try to do to the people -- with the people in his office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: First he'd listen to them. Then he would go to my office. I would have help him type up a report or a letter. The header would usually say: "The Executive Board of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" followed by the name of the company that the letter was being sent to. The title would be "request" and then followed by a very brief text, a very brief letter saying: "would you please see such and such person for an interview and give them if you can a job. We would very much appreciate that." Then this letter would be signed and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I take it it would be given to the people or person in his office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because you were his typist, his secretary, if you will, did you see him sign his name on few or many occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he signed these in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And because he signed those documents in front of you, are you acquainted with his signature?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Indeed I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll get back to that in a minute, but I want to go back to these requests that Mr. Brdjanin had you type out for him. Could you tell by the name that you were typing on the request whether they were a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: We had to give a name. We had to tell the manager of the prospective company who they were seeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you tell by typing the name what ethnicity they were? Whether they were Croat or a Bosniak, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, by looking at the first and last names I would normally make an assumption as to the ethnicity of the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And listening to Mr. Brdjanin's conversations with the people in his office, considering the documents that you typed on his behalf, was there any difference in the way that Mr. Brdjanin treated Serbs and non-Serbs in that two-month period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Everybody got the same treatment. He wanted to help everyone in some way, in whichever way he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you worked with Mr. Brdjanin, did you notice anything that was improper or incorrect about the way that he dealt first Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the Croat population in Banja Luka who came to see him in his office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No, no improprieties whatsoever, not as far as Mr. Brdjanin was concerned, the way he treated the people coming to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you worked with Mr. Brdjanin did you notice anything that was improper or incorrect in the way he dealt with the Muslim population of Banja Luka who came to see him in his office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No, never. He never treated anyone unfairly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the conversations that you had with Mr. Brdjanin, in private conversations, did he ever indicate to you any animosity towards the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that Mr. Brdjanin helped the citizens who came to his office deal with those issues. Did you -- the issues of housing, food, and employment, during this time period, did you ever -- were you having problems with your housing, your accommodation?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, what sort of problems were you having with your accommodations?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I had no accommodation. I don't have any accommodation even as we speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask your boss, Mr. Brdjanin, for any assistance in helping you get accommodations in July, August, and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to him twice, maybe more times. I'm not sure. I asked him to help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us how he would, with your assistance, type letters for Serbs and non-Serbs alike requesting assistance. Did he do anything like that for you?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No, not for me. He said he was sure that nothing would come of it and that he would not be able to help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there other members of the -- were there members of the executive council that were in the same building as you, the ARK executive council? Were they in the same building as you?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were, I believe, three other officers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were the people -- and do you remember who were in those three offices, which individuals?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: The president of the executive board, Mr. Erceg. His secretary. Mr. Zlatko Kelecevic, I believe he was there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg and Mr. Kelecevic, were they seeing people like Mr. Brdjanin was?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone that was trying to help the citizens like Mr. Brdjanin was in the offices in the building that you were in?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: The people that would come to see us would come to see us because of their problems, the problems they had. And the only person they spoke to was Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much of the day would be taken up by speaking to these people that were waiting outside his door when he came up?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Almost the whole time he was there at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever remember him turning anyone away because of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No. We wanted to give a hand to whoever we could, hoping that there wouldn't be that many people the next day. But you had the same situation every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he ever have meetings after the typical work day with people who were still in line or showed up late?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we were still in the office and it was past our working hours, we would just stay to hear them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've talked about your personal dealings, face-to-face dealings with the people who came to see Mr. Brdjanin. In your job as secretary, did you also answer the phone for him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would answer the phone for Mr. Brdjanin, would you refer phone calls to him?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you would refer phone calls to him, would you tell him the caller's name?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Well, whenever the caller actually said their name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And during the July, August, and September period that you worked for him, did he get phone calls from people who you could tell were non-Serbs based on their names?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he treat, for example, the people that you could identify as Croats when they called? Did he -- first of all, did he take their calls?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his -- generally speaking, how did he treat these people that you've identified as Croats when they would call?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: The same as whenever I told him that there was a Serb on the line waiting to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happens if you would get a phone call from a caller that by name you could identify as a Bosniak, a Muslim? How would he treat that caller?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: The usual way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any difference in the way that he treated phone callers based on their ethnicity? Did he treat Serbs, Muslims, and Croats the same?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time -- the three-month period that you worked for him, did you ever get phone calls from non-Serbs who called to extend thank-yous or gratitude to Mr. Brdjanin for helping them? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen, but there weren't too many calls of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We've talked about the phone calls that came from citizens. I want to talk about whether or not -- I'd like to have you talk about whether or not he got phone calls from any other individuals that you recognised as being involved in government. For example, did Vojo Kupresanin call?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's your definition of "several times"? How many times would that be over this three-month period?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Perhaps twice, perhaps three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Predrag Radic? Would he call?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your office ever call Mr. Radic's office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps about three times. The reason was to ask Mr. Radic to tell some of his own people to see these people who were coming to us to speak about their problems because we were no longer able to see everyone who came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cunningham. I think we better clear this up now. Did Mr. Brdjanin have one line, telephone line? And if that is the case, did he have to pass through you each time he needed to make a call? Or did he have a direct access to that line? That's question number one. Question number two, apart from the line that you were using, did he also have a separate direct line, another additional line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, Your Honour. The first question was if we had only one line. That's correct, we only had one phone that we used. I would usually answer this phone, and then I would pass messages on to Mr. Brdjanin. He did not have any other phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Nikola -- Mr. Erceg? Would he call?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: We were on the same floor, so there was no need for him to telephone us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Erceg meet? And if so, how often during this three-month period?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: We didn't have that much time. We didn't have enough time to see or speak to anyone apart from the people who were coming to see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you worked for Mr. Brdjanin, did General Talic ever call your office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever come visit in the office with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, no. Never. No military ever came to see us or called us on the phone, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Stojan Zupljanin? Did he ever call, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever come by?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there ever be any reason for your office to call him or his office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: I believe there was this one time we needed a car for Mr. Brdjanin to use to travel to a session of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that phone call involve?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: The only thing we talked about was about having a car secured for Mr. Brdjanin to travel because we had no official car to use on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we met yesterday, I asked you if you remembered the name Nenad Stevandic. First of all, do you remember --

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever remember -- and obviously, I know the answer to this. But do you recall Mr. Stevandic ever calling or coming by the office?

utterances.speaker: DRENKJA BERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.text: Yes.
